item.caption:
From Washington City to Logan, Utahns showed up Saturday for the fourth nationwide “No Kings” day of protests — but this time, participants voted, too.

The demonstrations were meant to mobilize people to cast their midterm ballots early ahead of Election Day on Nov. 3, organizers said.

In Salt Lake City, protesters marched from the Capitol to a ballot drop box by Salt Lake City’s Main Library.

Around two thousand people gathered at the Capitol ahead of the march, filling the steps with American flags, protest signs, music and costumes — and a recurring message that change starts at the ballot box. Many in the crowd had already voted, but some who brought their ballots proudly waved them in the air.

🔗: Read more at the link in our bio.

(✍️: Samantha Moilanen | 📹: @LandwehrPhotography)

item.caption: 🚨 BALLOT INTEGRITY: California Outlaws Arrests Within 200 Feet of Polling Locations on Election Day 🚨  Governor Gavin Newsom enacts a dedicated buffer zone designed to insulate voters from intimidation at the ballot box.  Key takeaways from the signed measure:The Legislative Buffer: California Governor Gavin Newsom formally signed a statute that criminalizes or bars law enforcement arrests within 200 feet of any voting site on Election Day.  Addressing Voter Intimidation: The law aims to prevent operations by law enforcement or immigration agencies (such as ICE) near voting precincts that could deter eligible citizens from turning out.  Visual Flashpoint: Viral posts juxtaposed Newsom against tactical agents wearing "POLICE ICE" gear, framing the legislation as a shield for vulnerable and immigrant communities against aggressive enforcement.  The National Debate: Voting rights advocates celebrate the rule as a vital safeguard ensuring unimpeded civic participation, whereas conservative critics argue that restricting law enforcement jurisdiction near public buildings could hinder response efforts during genuine criminal activity. 💬 Do you view this 200-foot buffer as a necessary protection against voter intimidation, or does it limit law enforcement too broadly?
